blocks.text: Content-agnostic blanks. Print as many as you need; use across any standard or subject.

blocks.when: students compare two people, events, or ideas.
blocks.why: the overlap makes shared traits explicit while the outer zones hold what is unique.

blocks.when: students weigh two categories, positions, or perspectives.
blocks.why: parallel columns keep the two sides balanced and organized.

blocks.when: students learn a vocabulary term or concept.
blocks.why: definition plus examples and non-examples builds durable understanding.

blocks.when: students trace what drove an event and what resulted.
blocks.why: separating causes from effects reveals historical relationships.

blocks.when: students order events to see change over time.
blocks.why: chronology exposes turning points and pace of change.

blocks.when: students make and defend a historical argument.
blocks.why: the claim–evidence–reasoning spine is how historians argue from sources.

blocks.when: students analyze a primary source before using it.
blocks.why: sourcing (context, audience, point of view, purpose) guards against misreading evidence.

blocks.text: One pre-labeled organizer per standard, matched to that standard's task and pre-loaded with sourced content. Tennessee connections flagged where a sourced tie exists.
US.01 — Homestead Act & the Transcontinental Railroad

blocks.when: students explain how two federal actions reshaped the West.
blocks.why: cause & effect separates the policy drivers from their human consequences.

blocks.tie: George Jordan of Williamson County, Tennessee — a Buffalo Soldier who received the Medal of Honor for distinguished service during westward expansion.
blocks.prompt: Local → National: how does Jordan's service connect to the westward-expansion story?

blocks.text: US.03 — Compromise of 1877, Jim Crow & Plessy v. Ferguson

blocks.when: students weigh the promise of Reconstruction against the reality after 1877.
blocks.why: a T-chart holds two sides — stated law vs. lived experience — side by side.

blocks.tie: Tennessee enforced Jim Crow segregation by state law. Ida B. Wells, who lived in Memphis, documented lynching and challenged disenfranchisement.
blocks.prompt: Local → National: how did Wells's Memphis work shape the national record?

blocks.when: students distinguish two strategies industrialists used to dominate markets.
blocks.why: the Frayer model pins a concept down with examples and non-examples.

blocks.when: students compare two waves of immigration on shared criteria.
blocks.why: a T-chart keeps origin, entry point, and reception parallel across the two groups.
